mstts:express-as.prosody: Welcome—I'm so glad you're here. Together, we're about to step into a space where freedom and responsibility aren't just lofty ideas, but the very foundation of what it means to be human. Have you ever wondered what life would look like if there were no instructions, no ready-made purpose handed down to us? That's exactly the journey Jean-Paul Sartre invites us on in his work, Existentialism is a Humanism. Imagine waking up to a world where meaning isn't waiting for you—it's something you have to create for yourself. In Sartre's view, there's no divine blueprint, no cosmic script; it's just you, standing in the middle of it all, faced with the exhilarating—and sometimes terrifying—freedom to choose who you'll become. And here's where things get really interesting: every single choice you make, no matter how small, doesn't just shape your own life. It echoes outward, making a statement about what matters for all of humanity. Sure, the weight of this responsibility can feel overwhelming. But it also opens up an incredible possibility—the chance to live authentically, to create your own meaning, and to turn even the most ordinary moments into something extraordinary. So, as we explore Sartre's bold vision together, let's stay curious and open to how these ideas might just change the way we see ourselves—and the world around us. Ready to begin? Let's dive in.

Chapter 1: Facing Criticism and Misunderstanding — Why Existentialism Needs Defending
Picture this: it’s a chilly evening in postwar Paris. People are shuffling into a lecture hall, their faces a mix of curiosity and skepticism. The air is heavy—not just from the cold, but with everything that’s happened: war, occupation, liberation. Everyone’s there searching for answers, maybe even a little hope.
Lately, you’ve probably heard the word “existentialism” thrown around—sometimes with a hint of scorn, other times just confusion. Folks in cafés and writers in newspapers call it a philosophy of despair, or claim it’s all about selfishness and chaos. There’s a lot of noise, and tonight, the time’s come to clear things up.
The room’s packed with all sorts—students hoping for something real, older listeners a bit wary, critics just waiting to pounce. The atmosphere crackles with tension and anticipation. The speaker steps up, fully aware of the swirling misunderstandings. But instead of launching into dry theory, they start with something deeply human: what it feels like to be misunderstood.
Haven’t we all felt that? Being seen for what we’re not, or having our motives twisted? Existentialism has weathered its fair share of this. People say it’s too dark, too obsessed with anxiety and meaninglessness. Some accuse it of being selfish, as if it tells us to ignore everyone else. And yes, there are even those who think it’s dangerous—like it wants to tear down morality and tradition.
You can almost feel how those words sting. Not just because they’re harsh, but because they completely miss the point.
Here’s what really matters: existentialism isn’t about sinking into despair or tossing out all values. It’s a way of responding when the old certainties we trusted—like religion, tradition, authority—have been shaken, or even destroyed. The war made that painfully clear. So, the real question isn’t “does life have meaning?” but, “how do we create meaning, now that the old answers aren’t enough?”
The speaker scans the room. You can sense the unease—people searching for something solid, searching for a way to rebuild their lives after so much upheaval. Existentialism, far from being a philosophy of hopelessness, actually points to a way forward. It tells us we aren’t defined by our circumstances or by what others say. Instead, each of us is responsible for shaping our own existence. Our choices matter.
And yes, that’s both freeing and a little scary. It means we can’t just blame fate or make excuses for what we do. But it also means real freedom is possible—the kind that’s rooted in the messiness of everyday life, not just lofty ideals.
See, the critics have only seen the hard parts of existentialism. They’ve missed the promise. The hope.
As the evening goes on, the speaker makes a promise: these misunderstandings will be tackled head-on. This isn’t about winning an argument—it’s about opening a real conversation about what it means to be human, especially in a world where nothing’s guaranteed.
The road won’t be easy, but it will be honest. And in that honesty, there’s a spark of hope we can all hold onto.

Chapter 2: Existence Before Essence—How People Define Themselves Through Choices.
Picture this: a child sitting quietly at a desk, pencil poised above a blank page. There’s no guidance, no rules, nobody telling them what to create. It’s wide open—full of possibility, but also uncertainty.
That’s actually a great way to start thinking about one of existentialism’s most powerful ideas: existence comes before essence.
Most of us grow up thinking everything has a set purpose. A chair? It’s made for sitting. A knife? Its job is to cut. Their reason for being is built in right from the start. For ages, people assumed humans were like that too—born with a purpose, a soul crafted by something greater, a destiny mapped out in advance.
But what if that’s not true? What if, instead, we’re more like that kid with the blank page—showing up in the world with no script, and having to invent ourselves as we go?
That’s the bold claim at the heart of existentialism. We exist first—we’re born, we act, we make choices. Only after that do we start to become something, shaping who we are through what we do. There’s no blueprint handed down, no essence that tells us who we’re supposed to be. Instead, every person is kind of a work in progress—defined, moment by moment, by their actions.
It’s a dizzying idea, isn’t it? And not everyone finds it comforting. Some people would much rather believe their life is part of a grand design, that there’s a path already set out for them. But existentialism asks us to let go of that safety net and face the reality of our freedom. There’s no one else to blame, and no fate to hide behind. Life’s meaning isn’t handed to us—we have to create it, one choice at a time.
Think about a young adult, torn between staying home to care for a sick parent or joining the resistance against an occupying force. There’s no rulebook, no higher authority to dictate the answer. It’s an agonizing decision, and whatever they choose, it doesn’t just shape their future—it shapes who they are. Right there, you see it: people aren’t defined by what they’re told to do, but by what they choose to do.
Most of the time, we don’t even realize this is happening. We slip into routines, follow habits, or do what’s expected—rarely stopping to wonder why. But existentialism insists that every action counts. Even the smallest decision is a brushstroke on the canvas of our lives. There’s no opting out of this responsibility. To be human is to be free, and to be free means owning what we become.
Honestly, this freedom can feel heavy—and even a little scary. It’s so much easier to think someone else is in charge, that there’s a plan we just need to follow. But existentialism offers a different kind of hope. It says that even without guarantees, we can still create meaning for ourselves. The blank page? It isn’t a curse. It’s an invitation.

Chapter Three: The Weight of Freedom—Anguish, Responsibility, and the Search for Meaning.
Have you ever laid awake at night, replaying the day’s choices and wondering if you did the right thing? Or maybe you’ve been in a conversation where, suddenly, you realize the words you just blurted out can’t be taken back. Sometimes, these moments come during a crisis, when the usual comforts or routines disappear, and you’re not sure what to do next. It’s in these times that the full weight of our freedom really hits us.
Existentialism has a word for this feeling—anguish. But it’s more than just anxiety or fear. It’s that deep, unsettling awareness that every single choice you make actually matters. Not just for you, but for everyone around you. Think about it: whenever you decide how to act, you’re setting an example—almost like you’re making a statement for all of humanity. That’s a lot to carry, right? And if things go wrong, there’s no one else to blame.
Imagine a teacher standing in front of their class, wrestling with a tough decision. Should they stick to the curriculum, even if it feels meaningless? Or take a risk and teach something that could really make a difference for their students? There’s no way to know for sure what the outcome will be. The pressure isn’t just about doing their job—it’s about living up to their own ideals. In that moment, freedom feels heavy and real.
Most of us try to dodge that feeling whenever we can. We look for someone else to take responsibility—maybe our parents, our bosses, or even traditions. Sometimes, it’s easier to tell ourselves that fate has a plan, or that someone else knows what’s best. But existentialism doesn’t let us off the hook so easily. It insists there’s no way to escape freedom, no one we can hand our lives over to.
Realizing this can leave us feeling “forlorn.” It’s a word that captures the loneliness of being truly free. Without a higher power or an outside authority to guide us, we’re left to find our own path. It’s a sobering thought, but it’s also where genuine authenticity begins. When we accept our situation for what it is, we can finally start living honestly—without hiding behind excuses or wishful thinking.
Then there’s despair, which is another effect of freedom. But here’s something important: despair isn’t about giving up. It’s about recognizing that we can only control our own actions, not what happens in the end. A parent might do everything possible to raise their child well, but there’s no promise it’ll all work out. A friend can offer support, but can’t force someone else to change. That doesn’t mean effort is pointless—it just means it has to be rooted in what’s actually possible.
So, when you feel the weight of freedom, remember: it’s not a punishment. It’s a chance to live authentically, to make choices that are truly your own—even if it feels a little scary sometimes.

Chapter Four: Living Without God—Creating Values and Meaning in a Secular World.
For centuries, so many people found comfort in believing that life’s meaning came from a higher power. There was this sense of order—a feeling that right and wrong were kind of woven into the universe itself.
But after war and upheaval, that certainty started to fade for a lot of folks. The big question shifted. Instead of asking, "What does God want?" people began to wonder, "What do I do when there’s no divine plan to follow?"
That’s really the challenge of living in a secular world. Without God, those old sources of meaning and morality don’t have the same hold. And sure, some might see that as a recipe for chaos—a world where anything goes and values are just up for grabs.
But existentialism? It takes a different angle. It says, if there’s no external authority, then you’re actually free to create your own values. Now, that freedom isn’t just an excuse to be selfish—it’s a call to real responsibility.
Picture someone facing a tough moral dilemma. Maybe it’s a worker tempted to cut corners, or a friend deciding whether to share a painful truth. There’s no commandment to look up, no cosmic judge to weigh the options. The choice has to be made, right here and now, with only your own conscience as a guide.
That’s both liberating and, honestly, a little scary. If things go wrong, there’s no one else to blame. But if things work out, you’re the one who made it happen.
Most people, when they’re faced with that kind of freedom, feel a sense of vertigo. It’s tempting to stick to old rules, to just do what’s expected, and try to avoid making mistakes. But existentialism insists—that’s not enough.
To live authentically means stepping up to the challenge of creating meaning in a world where nothing is guaranteed. It’s about taking responsibility—not just for your own values, but for how those values affect everyone around you.
Now, don’t get the wrong idea. This isn’t about inventing values out of thin air, or making choices on a whim. It’s about realizing that every decision you make is a statement about what matters—not just for you, but for all of us. When you choose honesty over deceit, or courage over fear, you’re really saying, “This is how I believe a human being should act.”
The stakes? They’re high. And the responsibility? It’s real.
Some people worry that this way of thinking leads straight to moral relativism—where anything goes and nothing really matters. But existentialism rejects that. The freedom to create values isn’t the freedom to do whatever you want. It’s the freedom to own the consequences of what you do.
It’s a tough standard, but it’s also full of hope. In a world without God, people aren’t lost. They’re free—to become whoever they choose to be.

Chapter 5: Authenticity and the Universal Impact of Personal Choices.
Have you ever noticed how, in those quiet moments before you make a decision, there's a kind of ripple effect you can almost sense? It's like, the choices you make—especially when no one's watching—somehow reach far beyond just you.
That's really at the heart of existentialism. The idea that when you choose for yourself, you're also setting an example for everyone else—almost like making a tiny statement about what it means to be human.
Imagine someone at work, deciding whether to speak up against something unfair. It's tempting to stay silent, right? Maybe it's safer, less stressful, easier to just blend in and let someone else deal with it.
But here's the thing: that moment isn't just about personal comfort. It's about drawing a line—showing what kind of world you want to live in, and what you’re willing to stand for. Whether you mean to or not, that choice sends a message.
Most folks think their actions are private, that what they do doesn't really matter in the grand scheme of things. Existentialism flips that idea on its head. It says, every single decision is like declaring, “This is what I believe is right.” And believe it or not, people notice. Sometimes it’s subtle, sometimes it’s direct—but your actions set the tone for those around you.
This brings us to authenticity. Living authentically means acting from your own values, not just doing what’s easy or what everyone else expects. It’s about having the guts to be honest—with yourself and with others—and not hiding behind excuses or blaming someone else if things go wrong.
Sure, it’s tough. Authenticity asks a lot from us. It’s not about being perfect—nobody gets it right all the time. Instead, it’s about owning your choices, learning from your mistakes, and never giving up on trying to do better.
In a world where nothing is guaranteed, that willingness to take responsibility—to keep striving for integrity—is maybe the closest thing we have to real certainty.
So, what’s the big takeaway? The universal impact of your choices is both a weight and a gift. It means you’re never insignificant. Every decision you make, even the little ones, has the power to shape the world in some way.
It’s a reminder to live with intention, to see how deeply we’re all connected, and to remember that what you do matters—not just for you, but for everyone around you.

Chapter 6: Engagement—Taking a Stand in a World That Won’t Wait.
You know, there’s this feeling that creeps in when you realize the world isn’t finished yet. History’s still unfolding, and each day adds another line to the story. For some, that thought can be overwhelming. Why even bother to act, when everything’s so uncertain? When the future feels like a thick fog?
But here’s where existentialism refuses to let us off easy. It doesn’t just suggest engagement—it demands it. To really live, we have to throw ourselves into the world, take a stand, and leave our mark. It isn’t just an option; it’s a must.
Picture this for a moment: someone sitting at their kitchen table, coffee in hand, scanning the morning news. The headlines? They’re rough—stories of injustice, conflict, people in pain. It’s so tempting to just look away, to slip back into private life and tell yourself, “Hey, this isn’t my problem.”
But existentialism has a different message. It quietly reminds us that just by existing, we’re already involved. We’re a part of this world, and like it or not, we share some responsibility for the way things are.
Most of us don’t realize how much our silence or inaction helps keep things exactly as they are. It’s easy to think that only the famous or powerful folks can make a real difference. But existentialism flips that idea on its head. It says every one of us, just by being alive and aware, is already engaged—whether we admit it or not. The only question is: how will we engage?
Think about someone who’s spent years feeling powerless. One day, they decide to volunteer at a local shelter. The work is demanding, and honestly, the results aren’t always clear. But just by showing up—by choosing to care—something inside starts to shift. The world doesn’t magically transform, but that old sense of helplessness begins to fade. Suddenly, it’s obvious: engagement isn’t about making grand gestures. It’s about being willing to act, even when you can’t predict what’ll happen.
Existentialism never promises that engagement will be easy, or that you’ll always see the results you’re hoping for. In fact, it warns us: you’ll face disappointment, maybe even frustration. But here’s what matters—the real meaning comes not from waiting for the perfect moment, but from jumping in, committing yourself to a cause, a project, a relationship.
Sure, the world’s uncertain. But the choice to engage? That’s always right there, waiting for you.

Chapter 7: Bad Faith—The Temptation to Hide from Freedom
Have you ever noticed how easy it is to slip out of responsibility, even in the tiniest moments? Maybe you nod along with the crowd just to keep the peace, or you chalk up a missed opportunity to bad luck. Sometimes, you even catch yourself thinking, "Well, that's just who I am."
Existentialism has a word for this little escape act—it's called bad faith.
Picture someone stuck in a job they really don’t like. They tell themselves there’s no other option—the bills need paying, expectations have to be met. It’s so much easier to believe that life is happening to them, instead of something they could shape. But if they’re honest, there’s this quiet, restless feeling that maybe that’s not the whole story.
Bad faith is when we pretend we’re not actually free. It’s denying our own power to choose—even hiding from the anxiety that comes with all that possibility. So we seek comfort in routines, old roles, and the same old excuses. Most people don’t even realize when they’re doing it. We start becoming the roles we play—parent, employee, citizen—forgetting that every one of those is a choice, not a life sentence.
Then, out of nowhere, something happens—a loss, a setback, or just a conversation that hits a nerve. Suddenly, you see the pattern and think, "Hold on, have I been living someone else’s life all this time?" That realization can be pretty unsettling. And honestly, the easiest thing is to go back to your old habits, to double down on what’s familiar. But existentialism suggests a different path.
Living in good faith means admitting that freedom is real—that you’re always more than just the sum of your roles. It’s about facing the discomfort of uncertainty, accepting that you might get things wrong, and carrying the weight of your own choices.
It’s not about walking away from your commitments, but choosing them—for real—with your eyes wide open.
The truth is, most of us don’t even notice how often we fall into bad faith. It’s a shield against the fear of freedom and a quick fix for the pain of regret. But existentialism insists: if you want to live authentically, you’ve got to face that fear, not hide from it.
The journey isn’t easy. But if you’re willing to step up, to own your choices and your freedom, that’s how you start shaping a life that’s truly yours.

Chapter 8: Hope and Action—Building Meaning in the Face of Absurdity.
You know, there’s this quiet kind of heroism in people who keep moving forward, even when life offers no promises. For a lot of us, realizing that the world doesn’t come with built-in meaning can feel overwhelming—maybe even a little hopeless. But here’s where existentialism flips things upside down. Instead of seeing that emptiness as a curse, it invites us to see it as an open door. An invitation to create meaning through what we do.
Picture someone who’s lost something or someone important. Suddenly, the old certainties are gone, and the future just looks blank. It’d be so easy to just give up, to slip into numbness. But maybe, instead, they start reaching out—calling a friend, trying new things, or simply showing kindness in little ways. The pain doesn’t magically vanish, but slowly, something new takes root. A sense of purpose—fragile, but real.
See, most of us are taught to wait for meaning to show up, as if it’s a gift from somewhere else. But existentialism says, no, meaning isn’t something you stumble upon—it’s something you build. It’s shaped by the choices you make, the risks you’re willing to take, the relationships you invest in. There’s no map, and definitely no guarantees. But in the act of trying, of caring, of creating, life starts to feel meaningful.
Let me share a quick story. There was someone who spent years searching for the “right” path, hoping for a clear answer. Eventually, they realized—there isn’t just one answer. The freedom to choose? It’s both a weight and a gift. And what really clicked was this: hope isn’t just a feeling you wait for. It’s a practice. It’s choosing to live, to try, even when things are uncertain, and refusing to let despair take over.
Existentialism doesn’t hand out easy comforts. It asks us to look straight at life’s absurdity, to accept that there aren’t any final answers. But it does offer a different kind of hope. The hope that, by living and engaging with the world, we can create meaning—not just for ourselves, but for others, too. It’s a hope that’s built on action, on being involved, and on having the courage to keep going—even when the road ahead isn’t clear.

Chapter 9: The Humanist Promise—Dignity, Solidarity, and Becoming More Fully Human
At the very heart of existentialism, there’s this deep respect for human dignity. In a world where there aren’t any guarantees, every one of us is called on to create meaning, to take responsibility, and to try to live as authentically as we can.
But here’s the thing—it’s not just a solo mission. Existentialism, at its core, is a kind of humanism. It’s a belief in the value and potential of every single individual.
Picture a community that’s just gone through a crisis. There’s fear, uncertainty, and plenty of grief. But alongside all that, there’s this powerful feeling of solidarity—a realization that everyone’s facing it together. People reach out, they support each other, they share the weight and start to build something new out of the wreckage. In moments like these, the true promise of existentialism comes alive.
You know, a lot of people think freedom is all about personal choice—something private. But existentialism sees it differently. Freedom is always something we share. It’s always tied to the freedom of those around us. To live authentically means recognizing the humanity in others, seeing that their struggles and hopes are deeply connected to our own.
Think about someone who’s spent years chasing their own goals. One day, they start to notice the needs of people around them. It’s a subtle shift, but it changes everything. Suddenly, it’s clear: being fully human means caring, connecting, and working to create a world where everyone’s dignity is honored.
Existentialism doesn’t promise us perfection. It’s honest about conflict, about suffering, even about failure. But it also reminds us that we’re capable of so much more—of courage, compassion, and creativity.
So, here’s the real heart of the humanist promise. It isn’t a guarantee. It’s a challenge—an invitation to become more fully human, to build lives and communities that reflect the very best of what we can be.

As we wrap up, let's bring everything together. Existentialism isn't just a set of ideas for scholars—it's really about how you show up in your everyday life. It's about being honest with yourself, finding courage in the tough moments, and staying engaged, even when things get complicated.
So, what does this all mean for you? Well, first, you're the one who shapes your own life through the choices you make. Sure, freedom can feel like a heavy load sometimes, but it's also an incredible gift. There aren't easy excuses—just new possibilities waiting for you.
Meaning? It's not something handed down—it's something you build, step by step, through your actions and how you care for others. Living authentically asks for honesty, a bit of courage, and the willingness to face the unknown. And remember, every decision you make doesn't just shape your own story—it sends ripples out into the world around you.
If you ever find yourself stuck at a crossroads, unsure of what to do next, think of existentialism as your compass—not a map with all the answers, but a way to find your own direction. The path is yours to choose, the meaning is yours to create. And you're not alone—everyone faces uncertainty, everyone shares in the hope and responsibility of making something meaningful out of life.
The world is still unfinished, and what you do really does matter. So, step forward with courage. Living authentically is about embracing both the risk and the reward of being human. In the end, it's less about finding the perfect answer, and more about living the question—fully, honestly, and together.
